One option is to send the DER-encoded `subjectPublicKeyInfo` as-is.

SPKI or even using the full end-entity certificate as-is might be easier to specify and to implement at the TLS level, but would move the complexity over to the TEE - not a great idea.

issues.title: Expand discussion of Extended Key Update
issues.author: yaronf
issues.body:
* Where do we add the Attestation messages.
* The EKU draft does NOT allow for additional messages in the key schedule, so we probably have to rewrite it to add requestor_attestation, responder_attestation.

comments.author: tireddy2
comments.body: EKU draft allows additional messages.

comments.author: yaronf
comments.body: You're probably right. But in plain TLS, the key schedule is defined to cover ALL messages between Client Hello and X, including new ones that are not defined by the standard. In EKU, the key schedule covers exactly the first two EKU messages.

comments.author: yaronf
comments.body: The second pair of messages does NOT serve the same purpose as Finished, they basically ensure that they're tied to the right EKU, under DTLS message loss conditions. But it's still good to include the Attestation messages in the hash for the same reason: to ensure they are not dropped.

issues.title: Evidence Does Not Prevent Attestation of Non-TEE-Resident Identity Keys (TIK)
issues.author: tireddy2
issues.body: It assumes that the TLS Identity Key (TIK) private key is generated and held inside the TEE. However, the protocol as specified does not prevent a platform from attesting a public key whose private key is actually external to the TEE.

comments.author: yaronf
comments.body:
It's a discussion we can have. My personal opinion is that we don't want to constrain the implementation too much. Others might disagree.

To me this is similar to the way we trust the TLS stack not to leak its session keys. Eventually we trust the software/system, but we can increase the level of trust by using open source, formally validated software etc.

comments.author: ionut-arm
comments.body:
I think the attestation should always bind to either the (exported?) attestation secret, the TIK public key, or both. And the evidence MUST provide verifiable proof that links up to the code producing the attestation secret, or handling the TIK, that the software which generated the evidence is doing this stuff correctly. Otherwise you just can't trust the attestation credential.

To me this is more similar to the treatment of TIK - you need proof from the peer that the TIK is under their possession. If the TIK just signed ClientHello instead of the longer transcript required for CertificateVerify, that proof of possession is not enough.

issues.title: Is attestation secret meant to be secret?
issues.author: ionut-arm
issues.body:
As per title: should we explicitly state this?

The secret _could_ appear in the Evidence in plaintext, so it could be accessible to the Verifier, for example.

comments.author: yaronf
comments.body: I don't think this is a contradiction. We do trust the Verifier to some extent, so we can say this is secret and at the same time share it with the Verifier. Even if this would allow the Verifier to impersonate the Attester this is still OK, because by definition, the Verifier can allow *anybody* to impersonate the Attester.

comments.body:
> Build fails (trailing spaces).

Fixed.
There's a back separator already, a few lines earlier. Please try to build the doc locally and hopefully it'll fail :-)
PAKE: add a ref to the draft.

Not quite: when we send Att is message flight 2 and 3, it is protected from a passive attacker by the DH exchange but still vulnerable to an active attacker. In that, Att is similar to the Certificate message.
ref to Section 4.2.6 of RFC 8446.
Thanks, fixed.
Added reference.
Added
I missed it, removed the paragraph.
No, the reference is https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-tls-pake/ (it's a very new draft but I agree it's relevant).
Fixed.
Let's be consistent: Reattestation (one word).

```suggestion
Reattestation is always associated with the completion of an Extended Key Update (EKU) exchange
{{!I-D.ietf-tls-extended-key-update}}. Extended Key Update injects fresh key-exchange input into

```

```suggestion
2. sends a new `Attestation` handshake message containing the updated CMW payload. The `Attestation` message MUST be sent immediately before the attesting peer's `EKU(new_key_update)` message.
```
Fixed in all the places.

No, please see sections 5 and 6 in the extended key update draft, In case of TCP, after the initiator sends `EKU(new_key_update)` the send keys are updated. In case of UDP, after the initiator receives the responder’s `EKU(new_key_update)`, the initiator will update its send key and epoch value.

I can add the following line:
The `Attestation` message MUST be sent immediately after the attesting peer's send key is updated.
Let's not use mixed cases please. Reattestation.
Fixed.

I think from a state machine POV it's easier to have Att before `EKU(new_key_update)`. It's also less confusing because you're still using the old traffic secrets to encrypt it (as we discussed, we cannot guarantee confidentiality against an active attacker anyway). Also, main_N+1 is already available at this point so I don't see why we couldn't have ATT *before* the EKU message. 

Lastly, including it before EKU(new_key_update) makes it simpler to include a hash of Att in EKU(new_key_update) itself - which is important for reliability, not for security. Think DTLS where the Att message gets dropped.

In our case, we need to send the Attestation message after EKU completes and after the “Use of Post-Handshake Authentication and Exported Authenticators with Extended Key Update” step in order to address the MITM attack described in https://github.com/tlswg/tls-key-update/pull/89, EKU by itself does not guarantee that both peers enter the same new key schedule; the authenticated transition is what detects any active interference.

Because attestation relies on Main Secret N+1, we only send it once that transition has been authenticated. I will reference that section directly in the draft to make the ordering clearer.

The value Main Secret N+1 already exists after the first message exchange so it can be used at that point. I agree both peers only advance the key schedule after message 3 and 4. I do agree that just like with the regular Finished, we should say that both peers should only update their view of the peer's attestation state after they receive and validate messages 3+4.

And again, I think including Att in EKU(NKU) is important for the reliability of the protocol.

NKU is defined purely as an acknowledgment that the traffic keys have been updated. It is intentionally not extensible, and overloading it with additional semantics would break that design goal. Because of that, I don’t think NKU is the right place to carry Attestation.

Since attestation messages use the standard DTLS handshake re-transmission mechanism, reliability problem is already solved by the protocol. 

The sequencing I am proposing is:

1) Run EKU.
2) Perform the authenticated-transition step to ensure no MiTM.
3) Exchange attestation messages.

Happy to refine the wording further, but this seems like the cleanest and least invasive design.
Isn't the last sentence here redundant, given the second-to-last sentence?
I'm not sure I follow why the EKU part is needed if you're already deriving from `Main Secret N+1`, which includes the main source of entropy that EKU gives you.
Do we need to expand on whether the opposite is also true (i.e., whenever there's an EKU => there's reattestation)?

> MITM attack described in https://github.com/tlswg/tls-key-update/pull/89

Can you please provide some more details about that attack? Can be somewhere out of band, or in the PR you link to, I can't follow how the attack works.

It is discussed in the https://github.com/tlswg/tls-key-update/pull/89, EKU provides fresh traffic secrets, but EKU alone does not authenticate that both endpoints derived the same updated keys. An attacker that temporarily compromises an endpoint may later act as an active MitM capable of interfering with the EKU exchange. Such an attacker can cause the peers to transition to divergent traffic secrets without detection, but cannot compromise the endpoint to derive secrets after the new epoch is established. To confirm that both peers transitioned to the same new key state, TLS 1.3 provides two mechanisms: Post-Handshake Certificate-Based Client Authentication and Exported Authenticators {{!RFC9261}}.
Yes, I will remove it.
TLS peers that support EKU may or may not support the draft but TLS peers which support our draft must support EKU.

(I really think we should meet, PR threads are not the ideal medium for this kind of discussion.)

> NKU is defined purely as an acknowledgment that the traffic keys have been updated. It is intentionally not extensible, and overloading it with additional semantics would break that design goal. Because of that, I don’t think NKU is the right place to carry Attestation.

I'm not proposing to extend NKU, I'm proposing to say that the Attestation message should (as a separate message) immediately precede NKU. So by the time you receive NKU it is clear if you have or haven't received Att.

> 
> Since attestation messages use the standard DTLS handshake re-transmission mechanism, reliability problem is already solved by the protocol.

I'm not sure how this could work unless we define an "ack" message, e.g. an empty Att message.

> 
> The sequencing I am proposing is:
> 
> 1. Run EKU.
> 2. Perform the authenticated-transition step to ensure no MiTM.
> 3. Exchange attestation messages.
> 

And my proposal is:
1. Run first exchange of EKU.
2. Run second exchange of EKU, where the client and/or the server can prepend an Attestation message to the NKU.
3. Now that both are authenticated, transition the TLS state and accept attestation (e.g. dispatch a callback to the application).

> Happy to refine the wording further, but this seems like the cleanest and least invasive design.

Updated text as follows:

Reattestation is tied to the completion of an Extended Key Update (EKU) exchange {{!I-D.ietf-tls-extended-key-update}}. TLS peers that require reattestation MUST support EKU, Reattestation is always associated with the completion of an Extended Key Update (EKU) exchange since reattestation depends on the key schedule update defined in the EKU draft.
In TLS, Derive-Secret is typically used with the corresponding handshake messages as its input. Using the EKU messages follows that established pattern.

Yes, we need a call to discuss this. 
DTLS already defines an implicit acknowledgement mechanism for handshake messages, so Att does not need to define its own “ack”. DTLS ACK would suffice. 

NKU is designed for single purpose: acknowledgment of key schedule advancement. Allowing arbitrary handshake messages to precede it creates an interleaving of unrelated handshake flows, complicating the state machine.

Can you please explain the threat with my proposal ?

Thank you Tiru, I was not aware of the DTLS mechanism and the ACK message. My remaining concern is about the state machine: suppose I'm the server and I just completed EKU with the client, and I'm expecting an Attestation message from the client. How do I know when to expect it, and when am I allowed to fail the connection if I don't receive it?

The answer to this question is clear in my proposal, because as soon as NKU is received I know that the handshake is done. That's why I think this option simplifies rather than complicates the state machine.

I added a new section "DTLS considerations", please check. 

I now understand the problem with the state machine, I see two alternatives:

a) The `Attestation` message MUST be sent immediately before the attesting peer's `EKU(new_key_update)` message. However, the receiving peer MUST NOT process Attestation until the EKU exchange and the authenticated transition step have completed. This ensures that attestation bound to Main Secret N+1 is accepted only after both peers have confirmed that they share the same `Main Secret N+1`.

OR 

a) we could introduce a new TLS handshake message ("attestation_request") that can be sent after EKU and the authenticated-transition step are complete. The receiving peer would then send a regular Attestation handshake message, using the freshly derived attestation secret.

Option A is what I was proposing, and it still is my preference. (With one minor change, the protocol allows for *both* peers to attest).

Option B is more complicated IMO. What makes it complicated is that in our design, either of the peers or both can send an Attestation message, and so the new state machine should accommodate all three of these options.
I updated the draft to use Option A.

```suggestion
The Attestation message MUST be handled using the existing DTLS handshake mechanisms for fragmentation, ordering, and retransmission to ensure reliable delivery.
```

Removed the whole ACK discussion because I think it's not needed now.

```
Att, NKU -->
         <-- Att, NKU
Ack?     -->
```

The first Att is acknowledged by the second flight. Should there be an explicit Ack for the second flight? Even if there is, it's the same as you'd have for NKU in regular EKU, and there's nothing new for Attestation.
This paragraph is also redundant now.
This paragraph may be true for DTLS 1.2, but my understanding of EKU in DTLS 1.3 is that it is self-contained, and the transition is completed without needing application-level mechanisms.
Yes, DTLS ACK is sent by the initiator for the NKU from the responder (see step 9 in https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-tls-extended-key-update/)
I don't get the comment, please elaborate.

My understanding is that EKU in DTLS 1.3 *does* guarantee that both peers transition to N+1, and an attacker can at most delay this transition.

Your text implies that a higher level mechanism (Exporter or post-HS client auth) must be used to ensure that, and I don't think this is the case. And if it is, it should be spelled out much better in the EKU draft.

Edited: sorry, I did not realize I should be reading the Editor's Copy of EKU. Having read it now, I honestly don't know what we should do now. Does the new Sec. 11 of EKU say that EKU is not fit for use in regular applications that are not using exporters?

Reading more of the new EKU draft: under your own assumptions (new Sec. 12.1), the attack could be mitigated if NKU were to sign the hash with each peer's TLS private key.

This would be a significant (and late) change. It also wouldn't be effective if your assumption that the private key is well protected doesn't hold. But I think it's worth a discussion. Anything we can do at the TLS level is better than putting the responsibility on the application.
Use of exporter is not mandatory, post-handshake server authentication can also address the problem.

Att, NKU  --> 
                <-- ACK for Att
                <-- ACK for NKU (optional to indicate NKU response will be delayed).
                <-- Att, NKU
ACK for Att -->
ACK for NKU -->

In DTLS, ACK is sent for handshake messages that is sent without any expected response.

I think you mean post-HS *client* auth, right?

And I think neither of them are likely to be used by most implementations. IMHO most will just set a timer to do EKU+reattestation at the TLS level every once in a while, without disturbing the application data flow.

So my concrete suggestion is to move this paragraph to be a section in the security considerations, and then we could either describe the attack and mitigations explicitly, or else just say that the security considerations of EKU (in particular, Sec. 12.1) apply here as well.
Updated draft.
